fieldNotes.title: Field Notes: The Section 16(2)(c) Interpretation That Did Not Exist
fieldNotes.source: Tax partner at Rao Krishnan & Co., a Chennai CA firm with a strong GST advisory practice
fieldNotes.story:
On 4 September 2025, a junior CA at the firm — newly qualified, four months in — used a general-purpose chat AI to draft the GSTR-3B for a logistics client with **₹74 crore turnover and a ₹38 lakh ITC mismatch** flagged by the GSTN portal. The mismatch was on inward supplies from a vendor whose GSTR-1 had not been filed for the period.

The junior asked the AI to draft an explanatory note for the client justifying the ITC claim. The AI obliged with a confident, fluent two-paragraph note citing **'the established CBIC interpretation of Section 16(2)(c) read with Rule 36(4), per Circular No. 183/15/2022-GST dated 27 December 2022, which clarifies that the recipient's ITC entitlement is preserved where the recipient has discharged its statutory obligations'**.

The interpretation did not exist. Circular 183/15/2022-GST exists, but it does not say what the AI claimed. The plain reading of Section 16(2)(c), reinforced by **multiple subsequent CBIC clarifications**, is the opposite — ITC is conditional on the supplier's tax actually reaching the government. The junior, trusting the citation looked specific (number, date, even a circular series), pasted the note into the client's working paper.

**The partner caught it on a 14-minute final review that evening.** She looked up the circular. The text bore no resemblance. *'If this had gone out under our letterhead and reached an ITAT bench, we would have spent the next 18 months explaining ourselves.'*

The firm's response was structural. Within 60 days, a **RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) pipeline** was built over the CGST Act, IGST Act, all CBIC circulars from 2017 onwards, and selected case law. **No AI tax output is now drafted without RAG retrieval, and every citation in any AI output must be verifiable against the retrieved source.** Junior CAs are trained, on day one, to copy any citation into the bare-act lookup before it leaves their screen.
fieldNotes.takeaway: An LLM without RAG is a confident-sounding witness with no documents. A real CA practice cannot use it for tax work. The fix is not better prompting; it is a retrieval pipeline indexed on the bare act.

bossBattle.title: Boss Battle: The AI-Drafted GST Notice Response — Spot the Fake Circular
bossBattle.setup:
It is **Friday, 1 May 2026, 3:30 PM**. **Anand** is in week 12 of the rollout. The pilot has expanded to GST advisory work. A long-standing client — a Pune auto-component manufacturer with **₹140 crore turnover** — has received a **DRC-01A intimation** from the GST department: alleged **₹22 lakh ITC excess claim** for FY24-25 on inputs procured from a vendor whose GSTR-1 was filed late.

Anand has used the firm's general-purpose chat AI (no RAG, against firm policy, but he is in a hurry) to draft a 2-page response. The draft is on his screen. **Partner Pramod** walks past, glances at it, and stops.

*'Anand. Read me the third paragraph.'*

The paragraph reads: *'The recipient's entitlement to ITC stands preserved per the principle laid down in **Circular No. 224/18/2024-GST dated 11 July 2024**, which clarifies that procedural lapses by the supplier do not, in themselves, defeat the substantive right of the recipient to claim ITC where the conditions of Section 16(2) are otherwise satisfied.'*

Pramod folds his arms. *'Walk me through how you wrote that. Stage by stage.'*

coach.name: Partner Pramod
coach.role: Senior partner, 22 years post-qualification, runs the audit and assurance practice

stages.prompt: **Stage 1.** Pramod's first question: *'Did you verify Circular No. 224/18/2024-GST exists?'* What is your honest answer — and what is your move now?

options.label: Yes, it sounds like a real CBIC circular series. The number format is correct. I am 90% sure it exists.
options.explain: 'Sounds like' and 'number format is correct' is exactly how the Rao Krishnan junior shipped a fake circular. The format being plausible is what the model is good at; the existence of the document is something only the bare-act source can confirm. 90% sure is 100% wrong if the 10% is real.

options.label: No. I will pull up the CBIC GST circulars page right now and search for circular 224/18/2024-GST. If it does not exist, the entire paragraph is fabricated and I rewrite from primary source.
options.explain: **Correct.** The verification step takes 90 seconds. The cost of skipping it is a notice response to the GST department citing a circular that does not exist. Pramod nods — this is the response he was hoping for.

options.label: I will ask the AI to confirm whether the circular exists.
options.explain: Asking the model that fabricated the citation to confirm the citation is a category error. The model has no way to know whether what it generated is real; it will confidently say yes. You need an independent source — the actual CBIC website, or a paid commentary database.

options.label: I will check with the senior junior who handled this client last quarter.
options.explain: Junior-CA tribal knowledge is not a primary source. The CBIC circulars page is. Use the bare act, not the bench grapevine.

stages.prompt: **Stage 2.** You check. The circular does not exist. The closest real circular (No. 183/15/2022-GST) addresses a related but different question. Pramod: *'Now diagnose. Why did this happen?'*

options.label: I used a bad prompt. I will rewrite it.
options.explain: Prompt rewriting will not fix this. Even a perfectly worded prompt to a model with no access to the CBIC corpus will hallucinate citations — because the model has no source to retrieve from. The fix is structural, not stylistic.

options.label: I used a general-purpose chat AI that has no live retrieval over CBIC sources. With no source corpus to cite from, the model fills the citation slot with statistically plausible numbers and dates. The fix is to use the firm's RAG pipeline that retrieves from the actual CGST Act, CBIC circulars, and case law before generating the response.
options.explain: **Exactly.** This is the correct diagnosis. A chat AI without RAG is recalling from training data and inventing the gaps. A RAG pipeline forces the model to cite only from retrieved passages, with verbatim quotes. Pramod almost smiles — almost.

options.label: The model was outdated. Newer model would not have done this.
options.explain: Newer models hallucinate too. They hallucinate more fluently. Model version is not the failure mode; the absence of a retrieval pipeline is.

options.label: The AI is unreliable for tax work. We should stop using it.
options.explain: Throwing out AI is throwing out the baby with the bathwater. AI with RAG, with verbatim quoting, with mandatory CA review, is genuinely useful. AI without those things is dangerous. Distinguish the tool from its setup.

stages.prompt: **Stage 3.** Pramod nods. *'Now rewrite the response using the RAG pipeline. What do you instruct it to do, specifically, to prevent this happening again?'*

options.label: *'Draft a response to the DRC-01A intimation.'*
options.explain: Same vague prompt as before, just pointed at a different model. You have not added the structural guardrails. The RAG pipeline by itself does not enforce verbatim quoting; the prompt has to demand it.

options.label: Prompt: *'Draft a DRC-01A response based ONLY on the retrieved passages provided in this context. For every legal position taken, quote the relevant section, sub-section, or circular text verbatim in quotation marks before applying it. Cite each source as "Section X(Y)(Z), CGST Act, 2017" or "Circular No. NNN/MM/YYYY-GST dated DD Month YYYY". If the retrieved passages do not address a question, return the literal string "INSUFFICIENT CORPUS — escalate to CA" instead of attempting to answer.'*
options.explain: **This is the move.** Verbatim-quote requirement, structured citation format, and a loud-failure mode when the corpus is silent. Pramod recognises the discipline — it is the same rigour he was trained to apply to opinion notes 22 years ago. Now you have applied it to AI.

options.label: Prompt: *'Draft a DRC-01A response. Do not hallucinate.'*
options.explain: Telling a model 'do not hallucinate' has been studied extensively and does not work. Mechanism beats instruction. RAG plus verbatim-quote requirement plus loud-failure mode is mechanism.

options.label: Prompt: *'Draft a response and add citations.'*
options.explain: 'Add citations' is exactly what got you the fake circular. The model added citations, just not real ones. The improvement is forcing the citation to come from the retrieved passage, not from the model's training data.

stages.prompt: **Stage 4.** Pramod's last question, the one that decides this lesson: *'The RAG-drafted response is ready. The client wants to file the DRC-01A response by Monday. Who signs?'*

options.label: The AI drafted it, you reviewed it, you sign as the prepare-er. The client signs as the assessee. We file Monday.
options.explain: An articled assistant cannot sign a tax response that goes to the GST department under the firm's name. The CA who signs is a qualified CA whose name and ICAI number appear on the engagement. The AI drafts; the junior reviews; the senior CA signs, full stop.

options.label: The AI drafted it. I reviewed it and verified every citation. Sundari did substantive review. You sign as the partner. The eval log entry captures every step. We file Monday.
options.explain: **This is the correct chain.** AI is a tool, not a signatory. Junior verifies citations against the bare act. Senior reviews the substance. Partner signs. Every step in the eval log. This is the never-ship rule applied correctly: AI never produces the version that is filed.

options.label: The AI signs digitally — this is the future of practice, partner.
options.explain: AI has no ICAI registration. AI cannot be disciplined by the institute. AI cannot be sued by the client. AI cannot sign. This is not a debate about future-of-practice; it is a current-law fact.

options.label: Skip the partner signature this once — we are short on time, the response is straightforward, and the eval log will document everything.
options.explain: An eval log records what happened; it does not authorise what should not have happened. The partner signature is the four-eye review's whole point. 'We were in a hurry' is the opening line of every ICAI inquiry transcript.

outcomes.perfect: Pramod uncrosses his arms. *'Anand, you got there. Verify the circular, diagnose the failure as architectural not prompt-level, rebuild on RAG with verbatim-quote discipline, and never confuse drafting with signing. Now go redraft. We file Monday under my signature, with your prep work and Sundari's review in the eval log.'* You have understood the most important rule in the entire course: AI never produces the version of a statutory filing that is filed.
outcomes.good: Pramod is satisfied that you can recover but corrects you on the prompt design or the signing chain. Re-read the lesson, especially the never-ship rule and the structure of a RAG prompt. Bring the redraft on Saturday morning.
outcomes.learn: Pramod is patient. *'Anand, this is the lesson. AI without RAG hallucinates citations. AI with RAG drafts; the CA signs. Re-read the lesson — the RAG move and the never-ship rule. The Rao Krishnan story is in the textbook because someone almost destroyed a 30-year practice on a Friday afternoon. Do not let that be us.'* The DRC-01A response gets redrafted on Saturday. Together.
